name: Purplish Lilac
lede: Purplish Lilac is a purplish shade of [[lilac|lilac]], one of Robert Ridgway's working names built by the plain grammar of modifier plus base color.

sections.title: A modifier, not a new color
sections.body: Purplish Lilac joins the modifier *purplish* to the base color [[lilac]], named for the flower [1][4]. Ridgway's 1912 plate XXXVII, hue 65-double-prime, places it high in lightness and low to moderate in chroma, LCH lightness 70 and chroma 16 [1][4]. The ISCC-NBS system calls the matching block, 240, 'grayish purplish pink,' close to Ridgway's point at a Delta-E of 3.1 [2]. The nearest named colors on file are [[deep-vinaceous-lavender]], [[dawn]] and [[french-white]], at 4.6, 4.8 and 5.1 ΔE [1][4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this shade, as photographed, in 0.08% of 23,781 paintings, just 18 paintings; within a single canvas it reads as a distinct area in 9 of them[3]. That makes it rarer than 69% of the archive's named colors [3]. It peaks in the 1900s, found in 0.3% of that century's 1,674 paintings, 3.8 times the expected rate, though the count behind that peak is small, 5 paintings [3]. Inside a painting, where it appears at all, it plays a light more often than a hidden color, 56% against 44% of its 9 appearances [3]. The earliest dated appearance is a 1600 painting, 312 years before the name's first documented record in 1912; the archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor and not a first [3]. In printed English the word 'purplish' peaks in the 1870s and rose fastest in the 1840s, counting every sense of the word [3].
